doc.title: Curtis Fuller — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Training the ear; transpositions and writing without a piano
summary: Fuller says he teaches students to sing chord tones, wrote trumpet parts for Thad Jones from his horn, and explains French horn, alto and baritone sax transpositions, mentioning Julius Watkins in Quincy's band.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Did they have similar work habits in terms of figuring that out?

Oh yeah. A student, sometimes, Eric can do it. That’s why the Suzuki method was so successful for a while, training the student’s ear. The student can actually train himself to hear. I’ll tell you, I’ll make a student to play a note, then I’ll tell him to sing or hum the third, fifth, and seventh. He knows that if he is going to be a writer or composer, he’s going learn there’s going to be a room sometime where there won’t be no piano. He’ll have to learn. Don Sickler would always tell me, “Damn, you and Thad Jones…” He said—ask him! I had written the whole trumpet
section thing with just the horn. I’d sing the note to him and tell him the line for the first trumpet, second trumpet. It’d fit in and he’d say, “Damn, you heard that?”

Well, it’s based on my horn. I don’t have to—I don’t carry a piano around. I do know, some instruments…the French Horn is a fifth in sound. You gotta hear that sound. Alto saxophone, being a sixth—actually, the alto can play—you can read the alto part as if you were playing the trombone! Just make the sharps natural, as long as it’s a minor interval. The baritone saxophone is just a big alto! (Laughs) Harry Carney is leading the section from the bottom, playing the same thing!
Well, you were, earlier and it was off camera, you were talking about your time in the Quincy Jones band. Julius Watkins was the lead.
Yes; he was the lead and the French Horn. Obviously, listen to the part (imitates Watkins’ part), French Horn would be the lead, if you know the lead tones. He may have written…
You characterized that instrument as a cross-­
As a cross between trumpet and trombone. I mean, the French Horns that you’re seeing in the band, you get two for the price of one if you got a French Horn player in there.
